svg.font-family: Roboto, Helvetica Neue, Helvetica, Arial, sans-serif
svg.title: How sprezzature-video works
svg.desc: Flow diagram. At the top, a film specification and the code it describes feed two lanes. The left lane checks the numbers: every declared claim against the place in the code that decides it, every number visible on screen against the declarations, and whether the film can be rendered again from a clone. The right lane checks the telling: the pitch in Kawasaki's order, and the mechanical half of the writing charter. Both meet in one outcome, the parts of a film a function can own, captions from measured audio, the poster baked as frame zero, and loudness levelled across a series.
svg.text: How sprezzature-video works
A film burns its claims into pixels, where nothing ever reads them again. This reads them.
A film specification, and the code it describes
scenes, narration, the numbers that will be on screen, and the repository they are about
Audit: are the numbers true
Every declared claim, against its source
a claim is a pair: the text on screen, and the place in the code
that decides whether it holds. The check runs against the film
that exists, not a description of it that can drift.
Every number on screen, against the declarations
this is the half that matters. Checking only declared claims
protects the numbers somebody remembered to declare, never
the one typed into a keyframe at midnight and left to go stale.
Can it be rendered again from a clone
three classes for every asset. A tracked copy proved equal
to its source, the output of a tool still on the machine, or a file that
exists in exactly one place. Divergence is reported, never
silently repaired.
Findings, exit 1 on any
five films said one chart count while the catalogue had held
another since September, baked into ten compositions
and five rendered files. Nothing, anywhere, was watching.
Audit: does it explain anything
The pitch, in Kawasaki's order
problem, then solution, then the one non-obvious thing that
makes the solution possible. Declared by scene index. It
catches no problem beat at all, a problem that arrives after
the viewer's patience has run out, and a secret sauce that is really
an inventory of what ships.
The prose, by the named machine tics
punctuation dashes, comma-plus-and, sentences that open
on a negation. One list per language: a French tic means nothing
to the English checker. Modals are counted and never failed
on, because a raw count confuses the senses.
What a regular expression can decide, and not
a step further
whether the problem is the right problem, and whether
a sentence earns its place, stay human questions. A green tick
standing in for a reading would be worse than no check at all.
Make: the parts of a film a function can own
Captions built from the narration script and the measured length of each audio file, not transcribed and not typed. The poster baked
as frame zero, because Slack, X and Discord regenerate their thumbnail server-side from the first frame whatever a poster attribute says.
And loudness levelled across a series.
Which tool grabs the frames sits behind a seam, because it is the least interesting decision here. Prose in a README gets re-read. A number
in a keyframe does not.
